title: Excluding one-sided randomized quasilinear-time log-space SAT
formal:
Is it true that no uniform randomized random-access algorithm decides Boolean satisfiability with one-sided error while using both quasilinear time and logarithmic workspace? More precisely, for every integer \(k\ge0\), is
\[\mathrm{SAT}\notin\mathrm{RTISP}\!\left[N\left\lceil\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil^k,\ \log_2(N+2)\right]?\]
Here \(N\) is the full binary input length. The two bounds hold simultaneously for one machine on every input and every sequence of coin flips. The error is allowed only on satisfiable inputs: each is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\), whereas an unsatisfiable input is never accepted.
why: This asks whether the known obstruction to extremely fast, very low-memory SAT algorithms survives useful one-sided randomness. An unconditional answer would advance lower bounds for a central NP-complete problem in a general computation model.
status_note: Source-open for the one-sided-error direction in the original Problem 5. The full source column, Diehl–van Melkebeek’s 2006 main statements and §§2.1–2.2 model conventions, and the 2021 Main Theorem 3/Definition 1 were read. The checked randomized results concern the opposite error direction or larger quantified/verification classes. Bounded later-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution of this exact randomized SAT target; this is not an exhaustive literature or independent proof certification.

progress.text: Randomized time-space lower bounds are proved for higher levels of the polynomial hierarchy and for tautology with one-sided error; the SAT error direction asked here remains distinct.
Problem 5 explicitly isolates randomized quasilinear-time logarithmic-space SAT with no error on unsatisfiable inputs.
New randomized time-space lower bounds apply to problems admitting Merlin–Arthur verification, with Main Theorem 3 retaining that larger problem class.

importance.reason: A sharply stated frontier for unconditional SAT lower bounds: it asks to handle fresh random bits in a resource regime already excluded deterministically, while preserving the error direction used by incomplete randomized solvers.

sentences: The input is an arbitrary explicitly written satisfiability instance.
A candidate algorithm may use fresh random bits, logarithmic working memory and time n times a fixed polynomial in log n.
It must never accept an unsatisfiable formula and must accept each satisfiable formula with constant probability.
Both resource bounds hold for the same machine on every sequence of random choices.
The target is an unconditional lower bound against every such algorithm; known opposite-error and larger-class results do not settle it.

definitions:
An input is an explicit Boolean 3-CNF formula: a conjunction of clauses, each containing at most three literals, where a literal is a variable or its negation. The empty clause is false and the empty conjunction is true. An assignment gives a Boolean value to every variable occurring; the formula is satisfiable when some assignment makes it true. Variable identifiers, signs, all occurrences and clause delimiters are written in a fixed self-delimiting binary list encoding. Identifiers can be taken from \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\), with unused identifiers permitted; \(N\) counts bits, not variables or clauses. Malformed encodings are no instances. There is no compressed formula or promise on the formula’s structure. The source explicitly permits 3-CNF satisfiability as its SAT target.

For definiteness, a random-access machine is a finite Turing-machine program with ordinary finite-alphabet work tapes and an address tape. When the address tape contains a binary index, one query step reads that indexed input bit; an out-of-range index returns a fixed endmarker. Writing, modifying and storing an address are charged ordinary bit operations. The input is read-only; all work tapes start blank. The total number of distinct work-tape cells visited, including the address tape and all temporary counters, is the workspace. This permits unrestricted repeated input access without charging the distance between input positions. Work-tape access uses ordinary moves. With only logarithmic work storage, the usual random-access work-memory or logarithmic-word variants can be simulated with polynomial-logarithmic time overhead and logarithmic space, so this quasilinear-time union is unchanged. There is no unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers, advice, oracle, external storage or extra catalytic tape.

At a random step the machine receives one fresh independent unbiased bit, at unit time cost. The random stream is available only in order and cannot be reread unless the machine stores the desired bits in its charged workspace. A random step is not a query to a random-access tape of reusable random bits. The machine eventually outputs accept or reject, without needing to output an assignment.

Write \(\ell_N=\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\). Membership in the displayed RTISP class would mean that one fixed machine and positive integer constants \(C,D\) satisfy, on every input and every random stream,
\[\text{time}\le T_N=D(N+2)\ell_N^k,\qquad \text{visited work cells}\le C\ell_N.\]
The harmless \(N+2\) makes the bound total at small lengths. Constants and \(k\) may depend on the machine, but not on the formula. In particular, this is a worst-case bound, not an expected-time or high-probability resource guarantee. At most \(T_N\) random bits can be consumed. Acceptance probability can therefore be defined as the fraction of strings in \(\{0,1\}^{T_N}\) that make the machine accept, ignoring unused trailing bits. For every valid satisfiable formula this fraction is at least \(2/3\); for every unsatisfiable or malformed input it is zero. A fixed positive success constant in place of \(2/3\) is equivalent by a constant number of repetitions, preserving the resource form and error direction.

The conjecture quantifies over every fixed \(k,C,D\) and every finite program. It concerns the simultaneous time-and-space class: a fast algorithm with large memory and a separate slow logarithmic-space algorithm would not supply the forbidden machine. The randomness is internal to the algorithm; inputs are arbitrary, not drawn from a specified distribution.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated nonexistence claim. A positive answer must exclude every uniform randomized machine, every fixed logarithmic-space constant, and every fixed polynomial-logarithmic time factor, with the specified one-way coins and error direction. A negative answer must give one machine and fixed \(k,C,D\), prove its time and space bounds on every random branch, and prove zero acceptance on no instances and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every yes instance. Bounds for deterministic machines, the opposite one-sided error, quantified formulas with extra quantifier alternations, a selected family of SAT solvers or expected resource usage do not establish this assertion. Neither an unproved separation such as P ≠ NP nor a conditional lower bound settles the unconditional target. The conclusion and probabilities have their exact stated meanings; no numerical approximation tolerance applies.

source_formulation.text: Problem 5 asks to rule out a randomized SAT algorithm using n times a fixed polynomial in log n time and logarithmic space, with possible error on satisfiable inputs only.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Problem 5, retaining its explicit direction of one-sided error

context_blocks.text: Randomized search for a satisfying assignment may miss an assignment that exists, while an accepted assignment can be checked for correctness. This motivates the source’s error direction. The target nevertheless ranges over all decision algorithms with this error behavior, not just procedures that explicitly search for or output an assignment.

Logarithmic memory holds only a small number of indices and counters. The input can be read repeatedly, but the time bound permits only a polynomial-logarithmic amount of overhead beyond its length. Randomness supplies fresh choices without furnishing free reusable storage. All three features—input access, memory and access to coins—matter.

Diehl and van Melkebeek prove polynomial-strength randomized lower bounds for quantified Boolean formulas with at least two quantifier blocks. Their theorem’s restriction excludes plain existential satisfiability. Higher-level quantified formulas cannot simply be substituted for the SAT instances in this card.

Their one-sided lower bound for tautology yields a bound for SAT with the opposite permitted error: always accept a satisfiable formula, but possibly accept an unsatisfiable one. Complementing outputs switches both the language and the error side. It does not yield the requested lower bound for algorithms that never accept an unsatisfiable input.

The 2016 source explains why ordinary space-efficient derandomization does not already settle the question. Its polynomial running-time overhead is too large for the known deterministic time-space lower bounds to contradict the resulting SAT algorithm. A qualitative polynomial-time simulation does not preserve the near-linear time requirement.

The 2021 paper extends time-space lower bounds to problems with randomized or quantum verification. Its Main Theorem 3 concerns linear-time Merlin–Arthur and quantum Merlin–Arthur classes against randomized logarithmic-space machines. Such a verifier receives an additional proposed witness; lower bounds for those larger classes are not automatically lower bounds for SAT.
